new_groups.label: The opening of Parliament, 30 November 1774: the King's speech, the Lords' debate and protest on the address, and the Commons' address of thanks
new_groups.definition: Three papers of the new Parliament's first days, as the colonial papers printed them from the London papers in January and February 1775: the King's speech from the throne of 30 November 1774, the House of Lords' rejection of an amendment to its address and the protest of the Lords who dissented, and the House of Commons' address of thanks. The King's and the Houses' own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The King's speech to both Houses of Parliament, 30 November 1774: 'a most daring spirit of resistance and disobedience to the law still unhappily prevails in the province of the Massachusetts Bay'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech from the throne with which the King opened the new Parliament on 30 November 1774: 'It gives me much concern, that I am obliged, at the opening of this Parliament, to inform you, that a most daring spirit of resistance and disobedience to the law still unhappily prevails in the province of the Massachusetts Bay, and has in divers parts of it broke forth in fresh violences of a very criminal nature'; he says he has taken measures for carrying into execution the laws of the last session and will withstand every attempt to weaken his authority over the colonies. The King's own speech.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The House of Lords on the address of thanks, December 1774: an amendment asking for the papers on America rejected, and the protest of the Lords who dissented
new_groups.definition: Printings of the House of Lords' proceedings on its address in answer to the King's speech: the motion to add that the Lords would ask for full information on the state of America before the House committed itself was rejected ('Contents 13, Non-contents 63' in one printing), and the Lords who voted for it entered a protest: 'Dissentient, Because we cannot agree to commit ourselves with the careless facility of a common address of compliment, in expressions which may lead to measures in the event fatal to the lives, properties and liberties of a very great part of our fellow subjects'. Counted by the protest. A report of the Lords' vote with the dissenting Lords' own protest.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The House of Commons' address of thanks to the King for his speech, December 1774
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of thanks for the King's speech that the Speaker of the House of Commons presented in December 1774: 'Most gracious Sovereign, We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble thanks for your most gracious speech from the throne'; the address answers the speech's points on America. The House of Commons' own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress's petition to the King of October 1774, as printed in 1775, and the colony agents' letter on its delivery
new_groups.definition: The petition to the King that the Congress at Philadelphia adopted in October 1774, which the papers printed in January and February 1775, and the letter of the colony agents in London, dated 24 December 1774, saying they had delivered it to Lord Dartmouth and that the King had received it graciously. The Congress's and the agents' own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress's petition to the King, October 1774: 'we beg leave to lay our grievances before the throne'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the petition to the King adopted by the Continental Congress in October 1774 and printed by the papers from January 1775: 'To the King's Most Excellent Majesty. Most Gracious Sovereign, We your Majesty's faithful subjects of the colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay, Rhode-Island and Providence Plantations, Connecticut, New-York, New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, the counties of Newcastle, Kent and Sussex on Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North-Carolina and South-Carolina, in behalf of ourselves and the inhabitants of those colonies who have deputed us to represent them in General Congress, by this our humble petition, beg leave to lay our grievances before the throne'; it lists the standing army, the new duties and courts and the acts of 1774, and asks the King's interposition. The Congress's own petition (its second petition of July 1775 opens with the same words and is a separate story).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The colony agents' letter from London, 24 December 1774: the Congress's petition delivered to Lord Dartmouth, and 'his Majesty had been pleased to receive it very graciously'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter that the agents of the colonies in London sent to the speakers of the assemblies on 24 December 1774: 'having received the Petition of the General Congress to the King, we immediately communicated the same to Lord Dartmouth, Secretary of State for the American Department', who told them that the King had received it very graciously and would lay it before his two Houses of Parliament when they met. The agents' own letter.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, December 1774: a member of a certain assembly asks the Lord Mayor how he liked the King's speech ('What speech?')
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of December 1774: 'A Gentleman who is a member of a certain assembly, asked the Lord Mayor, a few days ago, how he liked the King's Speech. What Speech? answers the Lord Mayor. Why, that printed speech in your hand, replies the member. You mistake, cries my Lord, this is no speech, it is the American death warrant.' An anecdote from the London papers (the Lord Mayor was John Wilkes), a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, 13 December 1774: 'The ministers, it is said, are much offended with General Gage', who acted on the defensive
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of 13 December 1774: 'The ministers, it is said, are much offended with General Gage. They certainly have great reason, for he has most grievously disappointed them. They had great hopes of throwing the blame upon him; but he acting upon the defensive has thrown it upon them.' A London report, at second hand ('it is said'), with the London writer's comment; a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, December 1774: transports sail for Ireland to take on four regiments; Major General Howe and Sir William Draper to go out as brigadiers
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of December 1774: 'A number of transports are sailed for Ireland, to receive on board the 22d, 49th, 55th, and 63d regiments. Major General Howe and Sir William Draper, are going out as Brigadiers on the Staff.' A London report, a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, 7 January 1775: Lord North is said to have declared that, far from the merchants' meetings being disagreeable to him, he wishes for as much information as possible on America
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London news of 7 January 1775: 'Lord North has publicly declared, that so far from the meetings of the American and West India Merchants being disagreeable to him, he, on the contrary, wishes for nothing more than as much information as possible on the American business to be laid before Parliament as soon as possible.' A London report of Lord North's words, a single paragraph of the papers' London news.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress, February 1775: the militia and minute men to perfect themselves in discipline, and the towns to encourage the making of fire-arms
new_groups.definition: Printings of resolves of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay of February 1775, with the address to the inhabitants that some papers print before them: since a large reinforcement of troops is expected and the province's destruction appears intended, 'RESOLVED, That the great Law of self Preservation, calls upon the Inhabitants of this Colony, immediately to prepare against every Attempt that may be made to attack them by Surprise'; the militia and the minute men are to perfect themselves in military discipline, and the towns to encourage persons skilled in making fire-arms and bayonets. Counted by the resolves. The Provincial Congress's own resolves.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The New York General Assembly, 23 February 1775: Mr. Thomas's motion on the necessity of appointing delegates to the next Continental Congress, and the vote
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract from the votes and proceedings of the General Assembly of New York of 23 February 1775: 'A Motion was made by Mr. Thomas, in the Words following, viz. Mr. Speaker, I Move that the Sense of this House be taken, on the Necessity of appointing Delegates for this Colony, to meet the Delegates of the other Colonies on this Continent, in General Congress, on the 10th Day of May next'; the debates that followed and the vote, in which the motion was rejected. The Assembly's own votes.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, March 1775: a captain from Antigua reports that Admiral Parry and his squadron are ordered to Boston
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of early March 1775: 'We are informed by a Captain of a vessel who arrived here a few days ago from Antigua, that Admiral Parry with the royal squadron under his command, on that station, has received orders to sail for Boston, where this gentleman will be second in command'. A report at second hand, from a ship's captain; a single paragraph of the papers' news (some papers print it after a paragraph on orders from Virginia for arms, which is counted apart).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The fighting of 19 April 1775 at Lexington and Concord, as the Massachusetts Provincial Congress published it: depositions, and its address to the inhabitants of Great Britain
new_groups.definition: The papers that the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay published on the first fighting of the war, the march of the King's troops to Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, as the papers printed them in May and June: the depositions it took and its address to the inhabitants of Great Britain, and the deposition of an officer of the King's troops taken prisoner. The Provincial Congress's publication and the deponents' sworn accounts.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Affidavits and depositions relative to the commencement of the late hostilities in Massachusetts Bay, with the Provincial Congress's address to the inhabitants of Great Britain (published May 1775)
new_groups.definition: Printings of the publication of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay: 'Affidavits and depositions, relative to the commencement of the late hostilities in the province of Massachusetts Bay: together with an address from the Provincial Convention of said province, to the inhabitants of Great-Britain', transmitted to the Congress at Philadelphia; the depositions are sworn accounts by inhabitants of Lexington and Concord, and the address begins 'Friends and fellow subjects, Hostilities are at length commenced in this colony by the troops under command of General Gage'. The Provincial Congress's publication of the deponents' sworn accounts; the accounts are the deponents'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The deposition of Lieutenant Edward Thoroton Gould, of the King's Own regiment, wounded and taken prisoner, on the march to Concord on 19 April 1775
new_groups.definition: Printings of the deposition that Edward Thoroton Gould, an officer of the King's Own regiment of foot taken prisoner, made before the Massachusetts authorities and that the Provincial Congress published: 'I Edward Thoroton Gould, of his Majesty's own regiment of foot, being of lawful age, do testify and declare, that on the evening of the 18th instant, under the orders of General Gage, I embarked with the light infantry and grenadiers of the line'; he describes the march to Concord and the firing at the bridge. The officer's own sworn account, as the Provincial Congress published it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Philadelphia, May 1775: John Brown, express from Ticonderoga to the Congress, reports that the fort was taken by men from Connecticut and Massachusetts
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report of May 1775: 'On Wednesday evening last arrived here, John Brown, Esq; from Ticonderoga, express to the General Congress, from whom we learn, that on the beginning of this instant, a company of about fifty men, from Connecticut, and the western part of Massachusetts' 'and joined by upwards of one hundred from Bennington', took the fort of Ticonderoga; it adds news of the Indians in Canada. A Philadelphia report of what the express said.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Livery of London's address, remonstrance and petition to the King, April 1775, and the King's answer
new_groups.definition: The address, remonstrance and petition that the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Livery of London in Common Hall presented to the King on 10 April 1775 against the measures for America, and the King's answer, as the papers printed them in June 1775. The City's and the King's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The address, remonstrance and petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Livery of London to the King against the measures for America (April 1775)
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'The humble Address, Petition, and Remonstrance of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Livery of the City of London, in Common Hall assembled' to the King: 'We your Majesty's dutiful and loyal subjects' 'beg leave to approach the throne, and to declare our abhorrence of the measures which have been pursued, and are now pursuing' against the colonies, and ask the King to dismiss his ministers. The Livery's own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The King's answer to the Livery of London: 'It is with the utmost astonishment that I find any of my subjects capable of encouraging the rebellious disposition'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the King's answer to the address, remonstrance and petition of the Livery of London, April 1775: 'It is with the utmost astonishment that I find any of my subjects capable of encouraging the rebellious disposition which unhappily exists in some of my colonies in North America'; he says he will continue to pursue the measures of Parliament. The King's own answer.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A gentleman in Providence to his friend in New York, 20 June 1775: a narrative of the contest of 17 June between the King's troops and 'our army' at Charlestown
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman in Providence (45 miles from Boston) to his friend in New York, dated 20 June 1775: 'You doubtless have been alarmed with divers Accounts of the Contest which happened on the 17th Inst. between the King's Troops and our Army; shall give you a Narrative in a few Words'; it tells how Colonel Putnam took possession of Bunker's Hill on the evening of the 15th and began an entrenchment, and gives the writer's account of the battle and the losses as he heard them. A private letter at second hand, from the American side, with the writer's own figures.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Addresses to General Washington and General Lee, June and July 1775, and Washington's answer
new_groups.definition: The addresses that the Provincial Congress of New York presented to General Washington on his way to the army, and that the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts presented to him and to General Lee on their arrival at Cambridge, with Washington's answer to the Massachusetts Congress, as the papers printed them in July and August 1775. The Congresses' and the general's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The New York Provincial Congress's address to General Washington, June 1775
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of New York 'To his Excellency, George Washington, Generalissimo of all the Forces raised and to be raised in the confederated Colonies of America': 'At a time when the most loyal of his Majesty's subjects, from a regard to the laws and constitution, by which he sits on the throne, feel themselves reduced to the unhappy necessity of taking up arms', the Congress welcomes him and trusts that he will lay down his command when an accommodation is made. The Provincial Congress's own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress's address to General Washington on his arrival at Cambridge, July 1775
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay 'To his Excellency George Washington, Esq; General and Commander in Chief of the Continental Army': 'The Congress of the Massachusetts Colony, impressed with every sentiment of gratitude and respect, beg leave to congratulate your Excellency on your safe arrival'; it describes the state of the province and of its army. The Provincial Congress's own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Washington's answer to the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, July 1775: 'Your kind congratulations on my appointment and arrival demand my warmest acknowledgments'
new_groups.definition: Printings of General Washington's answer to the address of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress: 'Gentlemen, Your kind congratulations on my appointment and arrival, demand my warmest acknowledgments, and will ever be retained in grateful remembrance. In exchanging the enjoyments of domestic life for the duties of my present honourable, but arduous station, I only emulate the virtue and public spirit of the whole province of the Massachusetts-Bay'. The general's own answer.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Massachusetts Provincial Congress's address to General Lee, July 1775
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay to Charles Lee, major general of the Continental army, on his arrival at Cambridge: it congratulates him on his safe arrival and says 'We admire and respect the character of a man who, disregarding the allurements of wealth and distinction his merit might procure, engages in the cause of mankind, in defence of the injured, and relief of the oppressed'. The Provincial Congress's own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress at Philadelphia, July 1775: its resolve on the restraining acts, its declaration of the causes of taking up arms, and its second petition to the King
new_groups.definition: Three papers of the second Continental Congress, as the papers printed them from July 1775: its resolve of 4 July on the two acts restraining the trade of the colonies, its declaration of 6 July setting forth the causes and necessity of taking up arms, and its petition to the King of 8 July. The Congress's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress's resolve of 4 July 1775 on the two acts restraining the trade of the colonies
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolve of the Continental Congress of 4 July 1775: 'Resolved, that the two acts passed in the first session of the present parliament, the one entitled "an act to restrain the trade and commerce of the provinces of Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire, and colonies of Connecticut and Rhode Island and Providence plantations"', and the act restraining the trade of the other colonies; the Congress resolves against them. The Congress's own resolve.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A declaration by the representatives of the United Colonies, 6 July 1775, setting forth the causes and necessity of their taking up arms
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'A Declaration by the Representatives of the United Colonies of North-America, now met in General Congress at Philadelphia, setting forth the Causes and Necessity of their taking up Arms': 'If it was possible for men, who exercise their reason, to believe, that the divine Author of our existence intended a part of the human race to hold an absolute property in, and an unbounded power over others'; it recites the colonies' grievances and declares that they have taken up arms in defence of their liberty and will lay them down when hostilities cease. The New-Hampshire Gazette prints only a report that it was read to the army, with its title (not counted). The Congress's own declaration.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress's second petition to the King, 8 July 1775: 'the union between our Mother Country and these colonies'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the petition to the King adopted by the Continental Congress on 8 July 1775: 'To the King's Most Excellent Majesty. Most Gracious Sovereign, We your Majesty's faithful subjects of the colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay', and the others, ask the King to procure a happy and permanent reconciliation, and that in the meantime measures be taken to prevent the further destruction of lives and to repeal the statutes that most distress the colonies. The Congress's own petition (its petition of October 1774 opens with the same words and is a separate story).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Burgoyne and General Lee, July 1775: Burgoyne's letter proposing an interview, and Lee's answer declining it
new_groups.definition: The letters exchanged by two former comrades on opposite sides, as the papers printed them in July and August 1775: General Burgoyne's answer from Boston to a letter of General Lee, proposing an interview, and Lee's answer from Cambridge declining it. The generals' own letters.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Burgoyne's letter to General Lee from Boston, July 1775: 'When we were last together in service'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter that General Burgoyne wrote from Boston in July 1775 in answer to one from General Lee: 'Dear Sir, When we were last together in service, I should not have thought it within the vicissitude of human affairs, that we should meet at any time, or in any sense, as foes'; he defends the authority of Parliament and proposes an interview on Boston Neck. General Burgoyne's own letter.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Lee's answer to General Burgoyne, Cambridge, 11 July 1775, declining the interview
new_groups.definition: Printings of General Lee's note from the headquarters at Cambridge, 11 July 1775: 'General Lee's compliments to General Burgoyne. Would be extremely happy in the interview he so kindly proposed. But as he perceives that General Burgoyne has already made up his mind on this great subject', he declines it, lest it give rise to jealousies. General Lee's own letter.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, July 1775: captains from Dominica and St. Kitts are said to confirm the report that the Parliament House was pulled down and Lord North fled to France
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report of late July 1775: 'Captain Lowndes, from Dominica, and Captain Hodge, from St. Kitts, confirm the above accounts' (of the Parliament House pulled down and Lord North fled to France), adding that a ship had arrived at St. Eustatia from Amsterdam with the same news. new_groups.definition: The address and petition that the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Commons of London in Common Council resolved on in July 1775, praying the King to suspend hostilities in America, and the King's answer, as the papers printed them in September and October 1775. new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The address and petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Commons of London in Common Council to the King, July 1775
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'The humble Address and Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled' to the King, of July 1775: the City's loyal subjects lament the hostilities in America and pray the King to suspend them and to adopt measures that will restore union and confidence. The Common Council's own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.definition: Printings of the King's answer to the address and petition of the Common Council of London: 'I am always ready to listen to the dutiful petitions of my subjects, and ever happy to comply with their reasonable requests, but while the constitutional authority of this kingdom is openly resisted by a part of my American subjects', he owes it to the rest of his people to enforce obedience. The King's own answer.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1775 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A letter from Albany, 2 September 1775: 'we hear there has been a skirmish near St. John's'; General Montgomery sets off toward St. John's
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Albany, 2 September 1775: 'By an Express arrived last Evening, we hear there has been a Skirmish near St. John's, between a reconnoitering Party of our Men in a Boat, and a Boat of Regulars, Canadians, and Indians'; it gives the general's account of the skirmish and says General Montgomery has set off with 1200 men for St. John's, to muster on the Isle aux Noix. General Washington's own address.

new_groups.definition: Printings of a report of the burning of Falmouth in Casco Bay by the ships under Captain Mowat on 18 October 1775, with the letter he sent the town: 'Canceaux, Falmouth, October 16th, 1775. After so many premeditated attacks on the legal prerogative of the best of sovereigns', he gives the inhabitants two hours to remove; the report gives the number of houses and stores burnt. A report from the town, with Captain Mowat's own letter.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1775 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 838 items found on the pages, 354 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and again with the families of 1774 over the 1775 pages (items_from_1774.json: 77 items, 8 in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found 895 runs, and the runs no finder item covers were read. Counted item by item (452 entries), 441 items meet the bar (count_1775.md). The items printed by every paper that survives for their weeks by the count were counted again by their own words with phrase searches over all 1,286 pages in both transcriptions; the admitted and chosen items were read on every page.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1775 5 to 7 papers survive for any item's weeks (6 for most of the year), so the bar is 4 papers for every item.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1775 has 7 catalogue series, which are 7 papers: the Connecticut Courant, Dunlap's Pennsylvania Packet, Gaine's New-York Gazette and Dixon and Hunter's Virginia Gazette run all year; the New-Hampshire Gazette survives in 39 issues, to 12 December; Purdie's Virginia Gazette from its first issue, 3 February; the Pennsylvania Journal for 27 December only. No 1775 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 2 misfiled RevX pages, on which no admitted printing stands.
